content: Supercooling refers to the process of cooling a liquid below its freezing point without it transitioning into a solid state. When a liquid is cooled below its freezing point, it will typically crystallize if a seed crystal or nucleus is present, as these act as a foundation for the formation of a crystalline structure. However, in the absence of such a nucleus, the liquid phase can persist until the temperature reaches the point where homogeneous nucleation of crystals occurs. Homogeneous nucleation can take place above the glass transition temperature, where the system exists as an amorphous (non-crystalline) solid. For water, this temperature is approximately 15 K (0 °C or 32 °F). However, under standard pressure, water can be supercooled to its homogeneous nucleation temperature, which is around 231 K (−42 °C). If the cooling rate is extremely rapid, on the order of 10⁶ K/s, the nucleation of crystals can be avoided entirely, and water transitions into a glassy state. The glass transition temperature of water is significantly lower and more challenging to determine, but it is estimated to be approximately 165 K (−108 °C). Glassy water can be reheated up to about 150 K (−123 °C). In the temperature range between 231 K (−42 °C) and 150 K (−123 °C), experimental observations reveal only crystalline ice. Supercooled water droplets are frequently found in stratiform and cumulus clouds. These droplets can abruptly crystallize into ice when they come into contact with the wings of passing airplanes, leading to the formation of ice. This phenomenon can interfere with the lift of the aircraft, which is why planes expected to operate in such conditions are equipped with deicing systems. Freezing rain is another example of supercooled droplets, which freeze upon contact with surfaces. The opposite of supercooling is the melting of a solid above its freezing point. However, this process is much more difficult, as solids almost always melt at a consistent temperature for a given pressure. It is also possible to superheat a liquid above its boiling point without it transitioning into a gaseous state. Constitutional supercooling occurs during the solidification of a liquid and is driven by compositional changes. This phenomenon results in the cooling of a liquid below its freezing point ahead of the solid-liquid interface. During the solidification process, the interface is often unstable, and the velocity of the solid-liquid interface must remain low to prevent constitutional supercooling. Supercooled zones are observed when the gradient of the liquidus temperature at the interface exceeds the thermal gradient. The slope of the liquidus phase boundary on the phase diagram is represented as ( m = partial T_L / partial C_L ). The concentration gradient is related to specific points, ( C^{LS} ) and ( C^{SL} ), on the phase diagram. The minimum thermal gradient required to establish a stable solid front is expressed mathematically and depends on these parameters.
